claim: Most models of infectious diseases, including tuberculosis (TB), do not provide results customized to local conditions.
source: Most models of infectious diseases, including tuberculosis (TB), do not provide results customized to local conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of infectious disease modeling presented in the introduction without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: In settings with little capacity for up-front investment, same-day microscopy had the greatest impact on TB incidence and became cost-saving within 5 years if delivered at $10/test.
source: In settings with little capacity for up-front investment, same-day microscopy had the greatest impact on TB incidence and became cost-saving within 5 years if delivered at $10/test.
evidence: This claim is supported by model projections presented in the manuscript, specifically from the results of the transmission model comparing different diagnostic strategies.

claim: With greater initial investment, population-level scale-up of Xpert MTB/RIF or microcolony-based culture often averted 10 times more TB cases than narrowly-targeted strategies, at minimal incremental long-term cost.
source: With greater initial investment, population-level scale-up of Xpert MTB/RIF or microcolony-based culture often averted 10 times more TB cases than narrowly-targeted strategies, at minimal incremental long-term cost.
evidence: This claim is based on model projections comparing broad vs. targeted diagnostic strategies across different settings.

claim: Xpert for smear-positive TB had reasonable impact on MDR-TB incidence, but at substantial price and little impact on overall TB incidence and mortality.
source: Xpert for smear-positive TB had reasonable impact on MDR-TB incidence, but at substantial price and little impact on overall TB incidence and mortality.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results showing differential impacts of the Xpert for smear-positive strategy on different outcomes.

claim: Currently, most published transmission models are either loosely calibrated to reflect global/regional outcomes or more tightly fit to specific epidemiological settings; in either case, model results may be difficult for local decision-makers in the majority of public health settings to utilize.
source: Currently, most published transmission models are either loosely calibrated to reflect global/regional outcomes or more tightly fit to specific epidemiological settings; in either case, model results may be difficult for local decision-makers in the majority of public health settings to utilize.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of transmission modeling without specific supporting evidence in the manuscript.

claim: Simplified models designed for in-country use by decision-makers, most notably the Spectrum suite of models supported by the Futures Institute, have been used to inform decision-making in the fields of reproductive health and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) for over a decade.
source: Simplified models designed for in-country use by decision-makers, most notably the Spectrum suite of models supported by the Futures Institute (Stover et al., 2010), have been used to inform decision-making in the fields of reproductive health and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) for over a decade (Stover, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature about the Spectrum models.

claim: Estimates from the Spectrum models are now routinely incorporated into official global and country-level estimates of HIV disease burden and intervention impact.
source: Estimates from the Spectrum models are now routinely incorporated into official global and country-level estimates of HIV disease burden (Brown et al., 2010) and intervention impact (Farnham et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature documenting the use of Spectrum models in official estimates.

claim: To date, simple, user-friendly transmission models have not been widely used for decision-making related to many infectious diseases other than HIV.
source: However, to date, simple, user-friendly transmission models have not been widely used for decision-making related to many infectious diseases other than HIV.
evidence: This is a general observation about the field without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Transmission models may provide guidance on both global and country-specific levels for diagnosis of active tuberculosis (TB).
source: Diagnosis of active tuberculosis (TB) is an example of a public health intervention for which transmission models may provide guidance on both global (Dowdy et al., 2006; Abu-Raddad et al., 2009) and country-specific levels (Menzies et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published modeling studies at different geographic scales.

claim: An unprecedented number of new diagnostic strategies for active TB are now recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), including same-day microscopy, microcolony-based culture techniques, line-probe assays for drug susceptibility testing, and Xpert MTB/RIF.
source: Specifically, an unprecedented number of new diagnostic strategies for active TB are now recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), including same-day microscopy (World Health Organization, 2011), microcolony-based culture techniques (Leung et al., 2012) such as the microscopic-observation drug-susceptibility (MODS) assay (Moore et al., 2006), line-probe assays for drug susceptibility testing (Bwanga et al., 2009), and Xpert MTB/RIF ('Xpert'), a molecular assay capable of providing results (including rifampin resistance) in 90 min with minimal human resource requirements (Boehme et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to WHO recommendations and published literature on these diagnostic tests.

claim: Xpert MTB/RIF is a molecular assay capable of providing results (including rifampin resistance) in 90 min with minimal human resource requirements.
source: Xpert MTB/RIF ('Xpert'), a molecular assay capable of providing results (including rifampin resistance) in 90 min with minimal human resource requirements (Boehme et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature characterizing the Xpert assay.

claim: TB program decision-makers must repeatedly determine when to invest in scaling up a novel diagnostic test, which test(s) to promote, and whether the implementation strategy should differ by epidemiological situation.
source: TB program decision-makers must repeatedly determine when to invest in scaling up a novel diagnostic test, which test(s) to promote, and whether the implementation strategy should differ by epidemiological situation (Cobelens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature on TB diagnostic decision-making.

claim: Without transmission models to provide locally relevant estimates of cost and impact under alternative implementation strategies, such decisions will be made without systematically considering the implications of available scientific evidence.
source: Without transmission models to provide locally relevant estimates of cost and impact under alternative implementation strategies, such decisions will be made without systematically considering the implications of available scientific evidence.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the role of models in decision-making.

claim: The authors created a flexible, simple modeling tool that allows non-expert users to define their local situation according to three key epidemiological parameters (TB incidence, proportion of new TB cases that are multidrug-resistant [MDR], and adult human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] prevalence) and local unit costs of TB diagnosis and treatment.
source: To aid in this decision-making process, we created a flexible, simple modeling tool that allows non-expert users to define their local situation according to three key epidemiological parameters (TB incidence, proportion of new TB cases that are multidrug-resistant [MDR], and adult human immunodeficiency virus [HIV] prevalence) and local unit costs of TB diagnosis and treatment.
evidence: This is a description of the tool created by the authors, which is the primary contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The tool incorporates user-defined estimates into a combined decision analysis-transmission framework to generate 5-year projections of TB incidence, mortality, and control costs for nine diagnostic strategies.
source: This tool then incorporates those estimates into a combined decision analysis-transmission framework to generate 5-year projections of TB incidence, mortality, and control costs for nine diagnostic strategies (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim describes the model's functionality and references figures showing the model structure.

claim: The 'Baseline' strategy uses sputum smear microscopy for each diagnostic attempt, with liquid-media TB culture only to evaluate smear-positive cases with a history of previous TB treatment for drug resistance.
source: 'Baseline': Sputum smear microscopy for each diagnostic attempt, with liquid-media TB culture only to evaluate smear-positive cases with a history of previous TB treatment for drug resistance. (Cultures in all scenarios trigger drug-susceptibility testing if positive.)
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'TB culture if previously treated' strategy uses sputum smear microscopy for patients without a history of TB treatment and smear plus liquid-media culture to diagnose TB in any previously treated individual with symptoms.
source: 'TB culture if previously treated': Sputum smear microscopy used for patients without a history of TB treatment; smear plus liquid-media culture used to diagnose TB in any previously treated individual with symptoms (regardless of smear status).
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'Xpert if HIV-positive' strategy uses Xpert MTB/RIF for HIV-infected patients only, with a positive test for rifampin resistance triggering treatment for MDR-TB.
source: 'Xpert if HIV-positive': Xpert MTB/RIF for HIV-infected patients only, with a positive test for rifampin resistance triggering treatment for MDR-TB. Xpert is assumed to be deployed at the district level, such that results cannot generally be provided during the same clinical encounter (Lawn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model, with a citation supporting the assumption about deployment level.

claim: Xpert is assumed to be deployed at the district level in the 'Xpert if HIV-positive' strategy, such that results cannot generally be provided during the same clinical encounter.
source: Xpert is assumed to be deployed at the district level, such that results cannot generally be provided during the same clinical encounter (Lawn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a model assumption supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The 'Xpert if HIV-positive' strategy is conceived as a 'best-case' scenario for HIV-targeted TB testing.
source: This strategy is conceived as a 'best-case' scenario for HIV-targeted TB testing: if individuals unaware of their HIV status are not tested with Xpert, this strategy will overestimate effectiveness, and if those unaware of their status are tested, it will underestimate costs.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model assumptions and their implications.

claim: The 'Xpert if Smear-Positive' strategy uses Xpert MTB/RIF for smear-positive patients only (i.e., for rapid DST), with a positive test for rifampin resistance triggering treatment for MDR-TB.
source: 'Xpert if Smear-Positive': Xpert MTB/RIF for smear-positive patients only (i.e., for rapid DST), with a positive test for rifampin resistance triggering treatment for MDR-TB.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'Xpert for All' strategy uses Xpert MTB/RIF for all patients.
source: 'Xpert for All': Xpert MTB/RIF for all patients.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'Xpert with Culture DST Confirmation' strategy uses Xpert MTB/RIF for all patients, but treatment for MDR-TB is only initiated if rifampin resistance is confirmed by culture.
source: 'Xpert with Culture DST Confirmation': Xpert MTB/RIF for all patients, but treatment for MDR-TB only initiated if rifampin resistance is confirmed by culture.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'MODS/TLA' strategy uses sputum smear plus microcolony-based TB culture (e.g., MODS or thin-layer agar, TLA) for all patients.
source: 'MODS/TLA': Sputum smear, plus microcolony-based TB culture (e.g., MODS or thin-layer agar, TLA) for all patients.
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'Same-Day Microscopy' strategy doubles the per-test cost of sputum smear microscopy in exchange for the ability to provide results to patients in the same clinical encounter.
source: 'Same-Day Microscopy': Double the per-test cost of sputum smear microscopy, in exchange for the ability to provide results to patients in the same clinical encounter (e.g., with peripheral, unbatched reading of sputum smears).
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model.

claim: The 'Same-Day Xpert' strategy doubles the per-test cost of Xpert MTB/RIF in exchange for the ability to provide results to patients in the same clinical encounter.
source: 'Same-Day Xpert': Double the per-test cost of Xpert MTB/RIF, in exchange for the ability to provide results to patients in the same clinical encounter (e.g., peripheral deployment, with greater costs reflecting lower volume per machine [Vassall et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is a definition of one of the diagnostic strategies evaluated in the model, with a citation supporting the cost assumption.

claim: The authors evaluated each of the nine diagnostic strategies in four emblematic epidemiological settings defined by TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence among new cases, and adult HIV prevalence.
source: For purposes of illustration, we evaluated each of these diagnostic strategies in four emblematic epidemiological settings, defined by TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence among new cases, and adult HIV prevalence:
evidence: This describes the approach taken in the analysis.

claim: The 'Reference/High-Incidence Setting' has TB incidence of 250 per 100,000/year (twice the global incidence), MDR-TB prevalence of 3.7% in new TB cases (the estimated global prevalence), and adult HIV prevalence of 0.83% (the estimated global prevalence).
source: 'Reference/High-Incidence Setting' (e.g., Southeast Asia): TB incidence 250 per 100,000/year (twice the global incidence [World Health Organization, 2012]), MDR-TB prevalence of 3.7% in new TB cases (the estimated global prevalence [World Health Organization, 2012]), adult HIV prevalence of 0·83% (the estimated global prevalence [UNAIDS, 2012]);
evidence: This defines one of the epidemiological settings used in the analysis, with citations supporting the parameter values.

claim: The 'Low-Incidence Setting' has TB incidence at entry of 8.9 per 100,000/year and declining, with similar MDR-TB and HIV prevalence as the reference setting.
source: 'Low-Incidence Setting' (e.g., United States, Western Europe): TB incidence at entry of 8.9 per 100,000/year and declining, with similar MDR-TB (as a proportion of new cases) and HIV prevalence as above;
evidence: This defines one of the epidemiological settings used in the analysis.

claim: The 'High MDR Setting' has TB incidence of 100 per 100,000/year, MDR-TB prevalence of 10% in new TB cases, and adult HIV prevalence of 0.83%.
source: 'High MDR Setting' (e.g., former Soviet Union): TB incidence 100 per 100,000/year, MDR-TB prevalence of 10% in new TB cases, adult HIV prevalence of 0.83%; and
evidence: This defines one of the epidemiological settings used in the analysis.

claim: The 'High HIV Setting' has adult HIV prevalence of 20%, TB incidence of 500 per 100,000, and MDR-TB prevalence among new cases of 3.7%.
source: 'High HIV Setting' (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa): Adult HIV prevalence of 20%, TB incidence 500 per 100,000, and MDR-TB prevalence among new cases of 3.7%.
evidence: This defines one of the epidemiological settings used in the analysis.

claim: A uniform set of costs was used for purposes of comparison across the four settings.
source: In each setting, we used a uniform set of costs for purposes of comparison (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the costing approach used in the analysis.

claim: Decision-makers can use the open-source model program to re-define any parameter according to their best local knowledge.
source: Although these four settings form the basis of the results presented here, decision-makers can use the open-source model program (included as Supplementary file 1, written in the open-source programming language Python, Version 2.7, www.python.org) to re-define any parameter in Table 1 according to their best local knowledge; a manual for doing so is also included as Supplementary file 2.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the model tool.

claim: The model has capacity to create non-equilibrium settings (e.g., declining TB incidence, increasing MDR-TB).
source: Capacity to create non-equilibrium settings (e.g., declining TB incidence, increasing MDR-TB) is included.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model.

claim: A web-based interface (flexdx.modeltb.org) allows users to input local TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence, HIV prevalence, and unit costs and provides customized results without the requirement to manipulate programming code.
source: We also provide a web-based interface (flexdx.modeltb.org) that allows users to input local TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence, HIV prevalence, and unit costs; this interface provides customized results without the requirement to manipulate programming code.
evidence: This describes the web-based version of the tool.

claim: The program corresponding to the web version is available on a public repository (https://github.com/JJPennington/FlexDx-TB-Web-Django).
source: The program corresponding to the web version is also available on a public repository (https://github.com/JJPennington/FlexDx-TB-Web-Django).
evidence: This provides information about code availability.

source: In the high-incidence setting, our model estimated TB mortality at 14% of incidence (95% uncertainty range: 7–20%, WHO global estimate 14% [World Health Organization, 2012]),

evidence: This is a model validation result comparing model output to published WHO estimates.

claim: In the high-incidence setting, the model estimated duration of TB disease at 1.2 years (95% uncertainty range 0.8–2.1), which is close to the global estimate of 1.4 years.

source: but unlike our model, WHO notifications often count failure and recurrence after default (in the same person) as two separate cases.

source: At steady-state in the model, 80% of incident TB was due to recent infection rather than reactivation.
evidence: This is a model output describing the proportion of TB due to recent vs. remote infection.

claim: In the high-incidence scenario, both the cost and impact of targeted strategies (culture for retreatment, Xpert for HIV-positive, Xpert for smear-positive) on incidence were small relative to broader diagnostic strategies (Xpert for all, MODS/TLA, same-day Xpert).
source: In general, both the cost and impact of targeted strategies (culture for retreatment, Xpert for HIV-positive, Xpert for smear-positive) on incidence were small relative to broader diagnostic strategies (Xpert for all, MODS/TLA, same-day Xpert).

claim: The incremental cost-effectiveness, in terms of cost per case averted, was similar across all strategies with the exception of same-day smear, which was cost-saving and had greater effectiveness than the baseline.
source: The incremental cost-effectiveness, in terms of cost per case averted (i.e., slope of the line from origin to each point in Figure 3), was similar across all strategies with the exception of same-day smear, which was cost-saving and had greater effectiveness than the baseline.
evidence: This is a summary of model results with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Same-day microscopy remained cost-saving by year 5 as long as same-day results could be provided at less than five times the per-smear cost of routine results (i.e., <$10/test).
source: Same-day microscopy remained cost-saving by year 5 as long as same-day results could be provided at less than five times the per-smear cost of routine results (i.e., <$10/test).
evidence: This is a model result from sensitivity analysis on the cost of same-day microscopy.

claim: Among the targeted strategies, Xpert for smear-positives was the most expensive but had the greatest impact on MDR-TB cases averted.
source: Among the targeted strategies, Xpert for smear-positives was the most expensive but had the greatest impact on MDR-TB cases averted,

evidence: This is a summary of model results comparing targeted diagnostic strategies.

claim: Among the broad strategies, culture confirmation of rifampin-resistant tests on Xpert saved costs with little reduction in effectiveness.
source: Among the broad strategies, culture confirmation of rifampin-resistant tests on Xpert saved costs with little reduction in effectiveness.

source: There was little difference between culture-confirmed Xpert and MODS/TLA,

source: and same-day Xpert was the most expensive and most effective strategy.

claim: In the high HIV setting, the impact of diagnostic interventions on TB incidence was diminished relative to the high-incidence setting, though the impact on TB mortality was similar.

claim: In the high HIV setting, the Xpert for HIV-positive strategy was substantially more costly, but also more effective, than in other settings.
source: Additionally in this setting, the Xpert for HIV-positive strategy was substantially more costly, but also more effective, than in other settings.
evidence: This is a summary of model results for a specific strategy in the high HIV setting.

claim: The impact of the 'Xpert for all' strategy on TB incidence was most sensitive to three parameters: the proportion of TB patients who would be empirically treated even if microbiologic testing yielded a negative result, duration of infectiousness before seeking care, and rate of reactivation from latent infection to active disease.
source: The impact of the 'Xpert for all' strategy on TB incidence (selected a priori as the primary outcome for sensitivity analysis) was most sensitive to three parameters, both in terms of absolute effects on impact estimates and partial rank correlation coefficients. These three parameters were: (1) the proportion of TB patients who would be empirically treated even if microbiologic testing yielded a negative result ('empiric treatment proportion'), (2) duration of infectiousness before seeking care ('pre-diagnostic delay'), and (3) rate of reactivation from latent infection to active disease ('reactivation rate').
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis identifying key model parameters.

claim: For the reactivation rate parameter, the key determinant was not the reactivation rate per se, but rather the proportion of active TB representing recent vs remote infection.
source: For this latter parameter, in-depth investigation revealed that the key determinant was not the reactivation rate per se, but rather the proportion of active TB representing recent vs remote infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of sensitivity analysis results.

source: If the empiric treatment proportion was increased from 25% to 37.5%, the projected reduction in TB incidence fell from 20% to 13%.
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis on the empiric treatment parameter.

source: By contrast, when only 12.5% of false-negative patients were started on therapy, 'Xpert for all' achieved a 31% reduction in incidence.

evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis on the reactivation rate parameter.

source: and 23% if reactivation was halved to 0.025% per year.
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analysis on the reactivation rate parameter.

claim: The projected 5-year reduction in incidence for the 'Xpert for all' strategy did not fall outside the range of 12–25% under variation of any other model parameter, up to 50% of that parameter's baseline value.
source: The projected 5-year reduction in incidence for this strategy did not fall outside the range of 12–25% under variation of any other model parameter, up to 50% of that parameter's baseline value (Table 1).

claim: Both costs and incremental costs were more sensitive to the cost of TB treatment than the cost of diagnostics.
source: Both costs and incremental costs were more sensitive to the cost of TB treatment than the cost of diagnostics.

source: For example, doubling the cost of first-line therapy (from $500 to $1000 per person) augmented the incremental year 1 costs for 'Xpert for all' from a 57% increase over baseline to a 77% increase,

source: and doubling the cost of MDR therapy (from $5000 to $10,000 per person) generated an 86% increase in incremental year 1 costs,

claim: Unit costs other than those for first-line treatment, MDR treatment, and the diagnostic modality under study in each scenario were not important determinants of incremental costs.
source: Unit costs other than those for first-line treatment, MDR treatment, and the diagnostic modality under study in each scenario were not important determinants of incremental costs.
evidence: This is a summary of sensitivity analysis results on cost parameters.

claim: Most transmission models of infectious disease control interventions present results that are not directly usable by decision makers because they are not customizable to local conditions.
source: To date, most transmission models of infectious disease control interventions present results that are not directly usable by decision makers because they are not customizable to local conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of transmission modeling.

claim: The flexible, user-friendly model of TB diagnosis and transmission allows users without modeling expertise to define an epidemiologic setting and unit costs, evaluating various diagnostic strategies in that setting in terms of population-level costs and impact.
source: We present a flexible, user-friendly model of TB diagnosis and transmission that allows users without modeling expertise to define an epidemiologic setting (according to TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence, and HIV prevalence) and unit costs, evaluating various diagnostic strategies in that setting in terms of population-level costs and impact.
evidence: This is a description of the model tool created by the authors.

claim: While this model cannot precisely replicate the epidemiological situation in any given location, it applies a standardized methodology across a wide range of settings, thereby illustrating important interactions between epidemiological parameters and projected impact.
source: While this model cannot precisely replicate the epidemiological situation in any given location, it applies a standardized methodology across a wide range of settings, thereby illustrating important interactions between epidemiological parameters and projected impact.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's capabilities and limitations.

claim: The model provides both a web interface for rapid calculations and full model code whereby users can change any model parameter for 'personalized' sensitivity analysis.
source: We provide both a web interface for rapid calculations and full model code whereby users can change any model parameter for 'personalized' sensitivity analysis.
evidence: This describes the two versions of the model tool available to users.

claim: The rank-ordering of diagnostic strategies may be relatively stable across epidemiological settings, but the actual population-level costs and impact differ dramatically.
source: Our model results suggest that the rank-ordering of diagnostic strategies may be relatively stable across epidemiological settings, but that the actual population-level costs and impact differ dramatically.
evidence: This is a summary of model results across different settings.

claim: This model serves as an example of how epidemiologists can provide decision-makers across a wide variety of local settings with rapid access to customizable 'first-pass' projections of cost and impact from transmission models without the need to construct tightly fitted models to represent all epidemiological settings.
source: This model also serves as an example of how epidemiologists can provide decision-makers across a wide variety of local settings with rapid access to customizable 'first-pass' projections of cost and impact from transmission models without the need to construct tightly fitted models to represent all epidemiological settings.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader implications of this modeling approach.

claim: In settings where little additional up-front investment is possible (<25% increase in TB control budget), same-day microscopy has the greatest impact on TB incidence with no increase in overall cost at 5 years, provided that same-day microscopy can be feasibly delivered for less than $10 per patient.
source: Specifically, in settings where little additional up-front investment is possible (<25% increase in TB control budget), same-day microscopy has the greatest impact on TB incidence with no increase in overall cost at 5 years, provided that same-day microscopy can be feasibly delivered for less than $10 per patient.
evidence: This is a policy recommendation based on model results.

claim: For settings in which containing MDR-TB is the most important consideration, Xpert for smear-positives has the greatest effectiveness for this outcome, but at substantial price and very little impact on overall TB incidence and mortality.

source: Inputs into the decision model include the probabilities of failure/recurrence, probability of empiric therapy, loss to follow-up before treatment, diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic delay, and economic parameters as shown in Table 1.
evidence: This describes the inputs to the decision analysis component.

claim: The primary outcomes under each scenario were TB incidence, TB mortality, MDR-TB incidence, and incremental TB diagnostic and treatment costs (during year 1 and at the end of the 5-year period) relative to the baseline strategy.
source: Our primary outcomes under each scenario were TB incidence, TB mortality, MDR-TB incidence, and incremental TB diagnostic and treatment costs (during year 1 and at the end of the 5-year period) relative to the baseline strategy.
evidence: This describes the primary outcomes evaluated in the model.

claim: By giving flexibility to change model inputs, the authors provide users the ability to conduct any sensitivity analysis desired.
source: By giving flexibility to change model inputs, we provide users the ability to conduct any sensitivity analysis desired.
evidence: This describes a feature of the model tool.

claim: For illustrative purposes, the authors conducted a series of one-way sensitivity analyses in which each model parameter in Table 1 was varied by ±50% of its listed value.
source: However, for illustrative purposes, we also conducted a series of one-way sensitivity analyses in which each model parameter in Table 1 was varied by ±50% of its listed value (for proportions, 50% of the difference between the value and either zero or one).
evidence: This describes the sensitivity analysis approach used in the manuscript.

claim: The primary outcome for sensitivity analysis was the change in TB incidence, comparing the 'Xpert for all' strategy to baseline in the high incidence setting.
source: Our primary outcome for sensitivity analysis was the change in TB incidence, comparing the 'Xpert for all' strategy to baseline in the high incidence setting.
evidence: This describes the focus of the sensitivity analysis.

claim: The authors conducted multivariable uncertainty analyses by calculating partial rank correlation coefficients between each natural history parameter and the outcomes of TB incidence, TB mortality, and 5-year costs.
source: We also conducted multivariable uncertainty analyses by calculating partial rank correlation coefficients (Kendall, 1942) between each natural history parameter and the outcomes of TB incidence, TB mortality, and 5-year costs.
evidence: This describes the uncertainty analysis approach with citation to the statistical method.

claim: The authors constructed 95% uncertainty intervals around estimates of outcomes in each individual country by simultaneously varying each model parameter by ±10% over a uniform distribution and each target value over its reported uncertainty range.
source: In addition, we constructed 95% uncertainty intervals around our estimates of outcomes in each individual country by simultaneously varying each model parameter by ±10% over a uniform distribution and each target value (i.e., TB incidence, HIV prevalence, and MDR-TB prevalence) over its reported uncertainty range.
evidence: This describes the approach to constructing uncertainty intervals.

claim: The authors constructed 10,000 simulations using Latin Hypercube Sampling and took 95% uncertainty ranges as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of outcomes in these simulations.
source: In this fashion, we constructed 10,000 simulations using Latin Hypercube Sampling (McKay et al., 1979) and took 95% uncertainty ranges as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of outcomes in these simulations;
evidence: This describes the simulation approach for uncertainty analysis with citation to the sampling method.

claim: These 95% uncertainty ranges are provided in the web-based version of the model for each country.
source: these ranges are provided in the web-based version of the model for each country.
evidence: This describes a feature of the web-based model tool.

claim: TB infection is modelled as a density-dependent process, a function of the transmission rate, total number of individuals in the population, number of individuals with 'less infectious' TB weighted by the relative transmission rate, and the number of individuals with fully infectious TB.
source: Thus, TB infection is modelled as a density-dependent process, a function of the transmission rate (β), total number of individuals in the population N(t), number of individuals with 'less infectious' TB (E, early active; Ahd0p, late active smear-negative; Phd0p, 'pre-treatment' smear-negative; and I, active on ineffective treatment) weighted by the relative transmission rate ζ, and the number of individuals with fully infectious TB (Ahd1p, late active smear-positive; Phd1p, 'pre-treatment' smear-positive).
evidence: This describes the mathematical formulation of TB transmission in the model.

claim: Three separate forces of infection are calculated for the three separate strains of drug resistance, with relative transmission weights.
source: Three separate forces of infection are calculated for the three separate strains of drug resistance, with relative transmission weights of φd.
evidence: This describes how drug resistance is incorporated into transmission dynamics.

claim: In order to generate an equilibrium population according to user specifications of TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence, and HIV prevalence, it is necessary to solve for the roots of a system of 100 ordinary differential equations, plus three additional equations to account for the user inputs.
source: In order to generate an equilibrium population according to user specifications of TB incidence, MDR-TB prevalence, and HIV prevalence, it is necessary to solve for the roots of a system of these 100 equations, plus three additional equations to account for the user inputs.
evidence: This describes the technical approach to model calibration.

claim: The authors accomplish equilibrium generation using the 'fsolve' routine in SciPy.
source: We accomplish this using the 'fsolve' routine in SciPy (www.scipy.org).
evidence: This describes the computational tool used for model calibration.

claim: To solve for the three additional equations, the authors first match each user input to a single parameter: TB incidence to the transmission rate β, MDR-TB prevalence to the relative reduction in transmission for MDR-TB φ2, and HIV prevalence to the HIV incidence rate θ.
source: To solve for these three additional equations, we first match each user input to a single parameter: TB incidence to the transmission rate β, MDR-TB prevalence to the relative reduction in transmission for MDR-TB φ2, and HIV prevalence to the HIV incidence rate θ.
evidence: This describes the technical approach to matching user inputs to model parameters.

claim: By solving for the roots at which the system of equations equals zero, the authors generate an equilibrium (steady-state) population that also defines β, φ2, and θ such that the user-defined targets are also met.
source: By solving for the roots at which this system of equations equals zero, we generate an equilibrium (steady-state) population that also defines β, φ2, and θ such that the user-defined targets are also met.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the model calibration process.

claim: Additional complexity is added to account for non-equilibrium in TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence by fitting an equilibrium defined by the user-specified target of HIV prevalence, and the user-specified 'initial' values of TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence, set to be 50 years in the past.
source: Additional complexity is added to account for non-equilibrium in TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence. We accomplish this by fitting an equilibrium defined by the user-specified target of HIV prevalence, and the user-specified 'initial' values of TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence. This equilibrium is set to be 50 years in the past; at this time, the system of equations is solved as above.
evidence: This describes the approach to modeling non-equilibrium scenarios.

claim: The authors allow for the parameters β and φ2 to be altered from their original values such that a second set of targets are attained after 50 years (start of the analysis).
source: We then allow for the parameters β and φ2 to be altered from their original values (corresponding to the equilibrium condition) such that a second set of targets are attained after 50 years (start of the analysis).
evidence: This describes the approach to modeling changing epidemiology over time.

claim: If calculated values at the end of 50 years do not match the user-defined targets, the parameter values are changed accordingly, and the model is re-run from equilibrium until the appropriate parameter value is identified that generates the user-defined TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence, within a relative tolerance of 0.05 in each variable.
source: If these calculated values at the end of 50 years do not match the user-defined targets, the parameter values are changed accordingly, and the model is re-run from equilibrium until the appropriate parameter value is identified that generates the user-defined TB incidence and MDR-TB prevalence, within a relative tolerance of 0.05 in each variable.
evidence: This describes the iterative calibration process for non-equilibrium scenarios.

claim: In the primary version of the model, automated non-equilibrium modeling is only implemented for low-incidence scenarios in which the user inputs a TB incidence of less than 50 per 100,000/year.
source: In the primary version of the model, this is only automated for low-incidence scenarios in which the user inputs a TB incidence of less than 50 per 100,000/year.
evidence: This describes a feature of the automated model calibration.

claim: In low-incidence scenarios, the model generates an equilibrium population 50 years in the past with a TB incidence of 50 per 100,000/year and reduces the transmission parameter β until the user-defined TB incidence is achieved 50 years later.
source: In such cases, the model generates an equilibrium population 50 years in the past with a TB incidence of 50 per 100,000/year and reduces the transmission parameter β until the user-defined TB incidence is achieved 50 years later (i.e., the start of the analytic period).
evidence: This describes the approach to modeling declining TB incidence in low-incidence settings.

claim: The approach to modeling declining incidence accounts for the fact that most low-incidence settings have substantially more latent TB infection than would be estimated by an equilibrium population with a very low TB incidence—thereby more appropriately reflecting a higher proportion of TB due to reactivation rather than recent infection.
source: This accounts for the fact that most low-incidence settings have substantially more latent TB infection than would be estimated by an equilibrium population with a very low TB incidence—thereby more appropriately reflecting a higher proportion of TB due to reactivation rather than recent infection.
evidence: This is a justification for the approach to modeling low-incidence settings.

claim: The authors include code (described in the user manual) that allows users to define high incidence scenarios that are not at equilibrium, as well as 'emerging MDR' scenarios in which the prevalence of MDR-TB is increasing rather than stable.
source: However, we include code (described in the user manual below) that allows users to define high incidence scenarios that are likewise not at equilibrium, as well as 'emerging MDR' scenarios in which the prevalence of MDR-TB is increasing rather than stable.
evidence: This describes additional features available in the model code.
